analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new oil and gas drilling leases off California's coast.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 42 House Democrats, never received a hearing or vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the nation's offshore leasing law to permanently prohibit oil and gas exploration and leasing in federal waters off California's coast, while leaving existing leases untouched. It was introduced in January 2019 and sent to the House Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, beachgoers, and tourism and fishing businesses in California, who avoid the risk of new offshore drilling platforms and potential oil spills along their shoreline. State and local governments that would bear cleanup and economic losses from a spill also benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: California coastal residents, tourism, and fishing businesses

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits oil and gas preleasing, leasing, and related activities in areas of the outer Continental Shelf off California's coast, overriding any other provision of the leasing law [S3].

Protects the coastline from the spill and industrialization risks that come with new offshore drilling, which fall on coastal residents, beaches, and fisheries rather than on the drilling companies [S2].
Leaves existing leases legally intact, so the ban targets future expansion rather than disrupting current operations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, which lose the chance to win new federal leases in Pacific waters, and the federal Treasury, which forgoes any future royalties from drilling in those areas. Consumers bear, at most, a marginal effect if domestic offshore supply is not developed.

drawbacks.text: A permanent ban forecloses any future domestic oil and gas production off California, along with the federal royalty revenue and energy supply that could come with it [S2].

The bill does not affect rights under leases issued before its enactment, so existing offshore operations off California could continue and the ban would not eliminate risks from those operations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated where the risk is: California's coastline, its tourism and fishing economies, and the taxpayers and communities who absorb spill costs. The cost is modest and diffuse — forgone potential royalties and some foregone energy supply — and the existing-lease carve-out means current operations are unaffected. On the record provided, the trade-off favors the public, though a permanent statutory ban does remove flexibility if energy conditions change sharply.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and its energy subcommittee, but the committee never held a hearing or vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Salud Carbajal introduced the bill on January 8, 2019, with 42 cosponsors, all California Democrats [S1] [S4].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S5].
On February 5, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it stayed [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a markup or floor vote and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests, which kept the possibility of future Pacific leases open, since no restriction on California offshore drilling was ever enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil interests kept future Pacific leasing open

for.name: Rep. Salud Carbajal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently prohibit oil and gas leasing off California's coast.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; on February 5, 2019 it was further referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources and received no further action.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 42 cosponsors were California Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the bill never reached a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would permanently close Pacific federal waters to new oil and gas leases, cutting the industry off from future exploration off California. The spill and cleanup risks of new drilling fall on coastal communities, putting the industry's interest directly against the public's on this issue.

industries.industry: California coastal tourism and commercial fishing
industries.note: Blocking new offshore platforms protects beaches, fisheries, and the coastal economies that depend on an unpolluted shoreline from the consequences of a spill.

industries.industry: Holders of existing California offshore leases
industries.note: The bill expressly preserves rights under leases issued before its enactment, so current operators keep their existing access to Pacific waters even under the ban.
